It designated the Governor of Bengal as the ‘Governor-

supervise and direct all operations of the civil and military
government or revenues of the British possessions in India.

that the Commander-in-Chief was not to be a member
of the Governor-General’s council, unless he was so
appointed. It laid down that the members of the Board of

revenues.
4.	 Which one of the following statement is incorrect
regarding the Charter Act of 1833?
(a)	 Governor General in Council were given the power to
legislate for the whole of the British territories in India.
(b)	 Governor General of Bengal became the Governor
General of India.
(c)	 It added a law member to the Executive council of the
Governor General, with voting power.
(d)	 The monopoly of tea trade with China was abolished.

Option (a) is correct: By the Act of 1833, the Governor
General in Council were given the power to legislate for
the whole of the British territories in India. These laws
were applicable to all persons, British or Indian foreigners
or others and to the servants of the Company. They were
enforceable by all courts in India.
Option (b) is correct: The Governor General of Bengal
became the Governor General of India. The Governor
General in Council was to control, superintend and direct
the civil and military affairs of the Company. Bombay,
Bengal, Madras and other regions were subjected to the
complete control of the Governor General in Council.

The Government of India Act of 1858, also known as the
Act for the Better Government of India, was a significant
piece of legislation during the British colonial rule in
India. It marked a major shift in the governance of India.
Here are some key features of the Act:
 Transfer of Power: The Act transferred the
governance of India from the British East India
Company to the British Crown. India became a formal
possession of the British Crown, and the British
government assumed direct control over India.
 Governor-General: The Act established the office
of the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy
of India. The Viceroy was appointed by the British
Crown and served as the representative of the British
monarch in India. The Governor-General of India
became the Viceroy. Hence, statement 1 is correct.
 Legislative Councils: The Act expanded the role of
legislative councils. It allowed for the creation of
legislative councils at the provincial (presidency) level,
where laws could be made, amended, or repealed.
These councils included both official and non-official
members. Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.
 Indian Representation: While the Act introduced
legislative councils, Indian representation was
limited and did not reflect the broader Indian
population. The majority of members were British
officials. Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.
 Financial Control: The Act gave legislative councils
limited control over financial matters, including
the authority to discuss the budget and finances.
However, real financial control remained with the
British government.

reforms, including changes in the judicial system. It
established high courts and district courts. Hence,
statement 4 is correct

that transferred the subject of ‘Cooperation’ from
the central Government of India to the Provincial
Governments. This change was part of a broader
framework introduced under the Act, known as dyarchy,
which aimed to decentralize certain administrative
responsibilities to allow greater provincial autonomy.

affected rural development, agricultural production,

efficient to manage these functions at the provincial
level, closer to the people involved.

19.	 With reference to the Government of India Act of 1935,
consider the following statements:
1.	 It abolished dyarchy in the provinces while providing
the adoption of dyarchy at the Centre.
2.	 It introduced bicameralism in all of eleven provinces.
3.	 It abolished the Council of India, established by the
Government of India Act of 1858.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
(a)	 1 only
(b)	 2 and 3 only
(c)	 1 and 3 only
(d)	 1, 2 and 3
Ans:	 (c)
Statement 1 is correct: The Government of India Act of
1935 abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced
‘provincial autonomy’ in its place. The provinces were
allowed to act as autonomous units of administration
in their defined spheres. Moreover, the Act introduced
responsible Governments in provinces; that is, the
Governor was required to act with the advice of ministers
responsible to the provincial legislature. It provided for
the adoption of dyarchy at the Centre. Consequently, the
federal subjects were divided into reserved subjects and
transferred subjects. However, this provision of the Act
did not come into operation at all.
Statement 2 is incorrect: It introduced bicameralism
in six out of eleven provinces and not in all provinces.
Thus, the legislatures of Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar,
Assam and the United Provinces were made bicameral,
consisting of a legislative council (upper house) and
a legislative assembly (lower house). However, many
restrictions were placed on them.
Statement 3 is correct: The Act abolished the Council of
India, which was an advisory body created by the 1858
Act to assist the Secretary of State for India.
Other features of this Act were as follows:
 It provided for the establishment of an All-India
Federation consisting of provinces and princely
states as units. The Act divided the powers between
the Centre and units in terms of three lists–Federal
List (for Centre, with 59 items), Provincial List (for
provinces, with 54 items) and the Concurrent List
(for both, with 36 items). Residuary powers were
given to the Viceroy. However, the federation never
came into being as the princely states did not join it.

20.	 Consider the following statements:
1.	 The Constituent Assembly as a Legislative body was
chaired by Dr Rajendra Prasad.
2.	 The last meeting of the Constituent Assembly of India
took place on January 24, 1950.
3.	 Sir B.N. Rao was the Secretary to the Constituent
Assembly.
How many of the above statement(s) is/are incorrect?
(a)	 Only one
(b)	 Only two
(c)	 All three
(d)	 None
Ans:	 (b)
Statement 1 is incorrect: The Assembly was assigned
two separate functions, that is, making of a Constitution
for free India and enacting ordinary laws for the country.
These two tasks were to be performed on separate days.
Thus, the Assembly became the first Parliament of free
India (Dominion Legislature). Whenever the Assembly
met as the Constituent body, it was chaired by Dr.
Rajendra Prasad and when it met as the legislative body,
it was chaired by G V Mavlankar. These two functions
continued till November 26, 1949, when the task of
making the Constitution was over.
Statement 2 is correct: The Constitution makers had
gone through the Constitutions of about 60 Countries,
and the Draft Constitution was considered for 114 days.
On January 24, 1950, the Constituent Assembly held
its final session. It however, did not end and continued
as the provisional Parliament of India from January 26,
1950, till the formation of a new Parliament.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Sir B.N. Rau was appointed
as the Constitutional advisor (Legal advisor) to the
Constituent Assembly. H.V.R. Iyengar was the Secretary
to the Constituent Assembly.

After the declaration of British Prime Minister Clement
Atlee about the end of British rule in India by June 30,
1948, the Muslim League started an agitation demanding
the partition of the country. As a result, on June 3, 1947,
Lord Mountbatten, the then Viceroy of India, put forth
the partition plan known as the Mountbatten Plan. The
plan was accepted by the Congress and the Muslim
League. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 was
enacted to give effect to the Plan.
The features of this Act were as follows:
 It ended British rule in India and declared India as
an independent and sovereign state from August 15,
 It provided for the partition of India and the creation of
two independent dominions of India and Pakistan with
the right to secede from the British Commonwealth.
 It empowered the Constituent Assemblies of the two
dominions to frame and adopt any constitution for
their respective nations and to repeal any Act of the
British Parliament, including the Independence Act
itself. Hence Option (a) is correct.
 It abolished the office of Viceroy and provided, for each
dominion, a governor general, who was to be appointed
by the British King on the advice of the dominion
cabinet. His Majesty’s Government in Britain was to
have no responsibility with respect to the Government
of India or Pakistan. Hence Option (b) is correct.
 It abolished the office of the Secretary of State for
India and transferred his functions to the Secretary
of State for Commonwealth Affairs. Hence Option (c)
is correct.
 It proclaimed the lapse of British paramountcy over
the Indian princely states and treaty relations with
tribal areas from August 15, 1947.
 It granted freedom to the Indian princely states
either to join the Dominion of India or the Dominion
of Pakistan or to remain independent.
Government of India Act of 1935 provided for the
establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of

is incorrect.

1.	 Consider the following statements regarding a
Constituent Assembly:
1.	 The idea of a Constituent Assembly for India was put
forward by M.N. Roy for the first time.
2.	 It was constituted under the scheme formulated by
the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a)	 1 only
(b)	 2 only
(c)	 Both 1 and 2
(d)	 Neither 1 nor 2
Ans:	 (c)

communist movement in India. In 1934, he put forward
the Idea of a Constituent Assembly for India for the first
time. In 1935, the Indian National Congress (INC), for the

frame a Constitution for India. In 1938, Jawaharlal Nehru,

franchise.

was constituted in November 1946 under the scheme
formulated by the Cabinet Mission Plan. While it rejected

scheme for the Constituent Assembly which more or less
satisfied the Muslim League.
